message.reasoning:
I am playing Monopoly as player p4.

Evaluating a trade offer from p1. I would give up St. James Place for $20 and Connecticut Avenue. That completes two of three light blue properties, but I still need Vermont. p1 would gain St. James Place and Tennessee Avenue.

This swap is a clear loss. St. James Place and Tennessee Avenue are the most valuable orange properties due to jail proximity, while Connecticut is a weaker light blue. I will reject the offer.

I will reject the offer outright. I am now considering a counter-offer that gives p1 Connecticut Avenue without requiring St. James Place.

A $350 cash offer for Connecticut would leave me with $870. That is enough to buy properties later, but two light blues are still weaker than St. James Place.

Overpaying for Connecticut would tie up cash needed for New York, Vermont, and railroads. The property is also strategically stranded for p1 without Oriental Avenue. p1's real goal is clearly the orange monopoly path.

A cash-only counter for Connecticut could run $300 to $360. I will either reject the offer or explain that I will not trade orange properties for light blues. Refusing all trades keeps both players with one orange and one light blue, leaving New York unowned. Accepting would give p1 two oranges and me two light blues, but they would hold a stronger position.

The $20 offer is insulting. Face value shows a $40 loss, and I would give up the stronger orange group for a weaker light blue set. A counter demanding Connecticut plus Tennessee is unrealistic.

A counter demanding both Tennessee and Connecticut would give me two orange and two light blue monopolies, but p1 would never accept that. The swap offer reveals they value St. James Place far more than Connecticut Avenue plus cash.

A cash-only offer for Connecticut will likely fail again, since p1 is using it as a bargaining chip for St. James Place. I will reject the trade and keep St. James Place as a blocker on their orange set. I will respond with a polite but firm message that leaves the door open for a future cash deal without signaling weakness.
